origin_region: Yunnan · Pu'er · Zhenyuan · Ailao Shan · Qianjiazhai
cultivar: Wild-type and seed-grown Yunnan large-leaf trees of the Qianjiazhai forest and surrounding villages
processing: Raw pu-erh: pan-fired, rolled and sun-dried maocha, sold loose or pressed lightly into cakes; forest lots are processed in small batches and often kept loose.
harvest_season: Spring (April into early May at this altitude) for the main harvest; autumn tea from the village gardens is also sold.
appearance_dry: Long, dark, lightly twisted leaves with long thin buds and reddish stems, pressed loosely or sold loose.
appearance_liquor: Pale gold, clear, slightly oily on the surface.
appearance_wet: Long, soft leaves of uneven sizes, olive to yellow-green, with the thin leaf of forest trees mixed in.
taste_profile: Cool, sweet and gentle, with mountain honey, wildflowers and a faint herbal-sour edge typical of forest tea, very low bitterness, a light body and a long, fresh aftertaste.

brewing.notes: Rinse once. Gentle tea; brew it with a full 7–8 g in porcelain and let the late steeps run long. Not a tea for clay or for heavy-handed gongfu.

vintage_note: Sold by spring harvest year, mostly as loose maocha or small loosely pressed cakes from Zhenyuan producers, and labelled either 'wild' (yesheng, from forest trees) or 'gushu' (old village gardens). It is a tea to drink young (1–5 years) for its cool fragrance; it rounds into honey over 5–10 years but there is no aged Qianjiazhai market, so everything on sale is roughly 2010–2025 and dry-stored. Because the forest is a protected reserve and the famous ancient tree is off limits, be suspicious of large quantities of 'Qianjiazhai wild tea' at low prices.
description:
Qianjiazhai is a remote village and forest area in Zhenyuan County, Pu'er prefecture, high in the Ailao Shan nature reserve, and it is where the celebrated 'wild tea king' stands: a forest tea tree at around 2,450 m that was surveyed in the 1990s and is commonly claimed to be about 2,700 years old. Whatever the exact age, the tree made the name, and Qianjiazhai became the flagship of Ailao Shan wild tea.

The tea itself comes from two sources: true forest trees scattered through the reserve, picked sparingly and sold in tiny lots, and seed-grown village gardens around the settlement. Both are processed as ordinary sheng, pan-fired, rolled and sun-dried, but the forest leaf is thinner and darker, and much of it is sold loose because pressing such small amounts is not worth it.

In the cup Qianjiazhai is cool and quiet: mountain honey, wildflowers, a faint herbal or even slightly sour edge that is typical of forest tea, almost no bitterness and a fresh finish that lasts. The body is light. It needs a gentle hand and porcelain, and it rewards patience across ten or more steeps rather than impact in the first three.

Sold by spring year, with 'wild' or 'gushu' as the key word on the label, and mostly by small Zhenyuan producers and the Western vendors who buy from them. Real forest tea is scarce by definition, so the honest version of this tea is a few hundred grams of loose leaf, not a pallet of cakes. The village-garden tea sold as Qianjiazhai gushu is a fair and pleasant buy.

It makes a quiet, almost meditative session; if you want the same coolness with more body, a Zhenyuan tea from the Wuliang side of the county (Laowushan) is the next thing to try.
sources_note: The 2,700-year age of the Qianjiazhai 'No. 1' wild tea tree is the commonly quoted figure from a 1990s survey and is stated as a claim; altitude figures around 2,450 m are from the same reports.
